Design a wireframe DNA origami octahedron: a hollow, regular octahedron (6 vertices, 12 edges) whose edges are
each a bundle of two parallel helices (a double-crossover, "DX", edge), joined at its six vertices. Each edge
should be about 84 bp (about 29 nm) of duplex, and the octahedron about 35 nm along each edge from vertex to
vertex. Four edges meet at every vertex.

Requirements:
- exactly 24 helices: two per edge, the pair side by side and joined by staple crossovers along the edge
- 80-88 base pairs on every helix
- each edge's two helices form one helix group; groups are positioned and rotated (yaw, pitch, roll) so the
  twelve edges lie along the edges of an octahedron
- every vertex joins its four edges with the scaffold or staples
- a single scaffold strand that is a contiguous fragment of M13mp18, 1950-2350 nt long
- at least 90% of the scaffold base-paired to staples (the rest are short unpaired loops at the vertices)
- every staple 18-60 nt long

Shape: the design's nucleotides must trace an octahedron with 35 nm edges. Precisely, after the best rigid fit,
at least 90% of the nucleotides must lie within 3.5 nm of an octahedron edge, and nearly every point along the
middle of each edge (more than 6 nm from its vertices) must have a nucleotide within 3.5 nm.

Save your design under /designs/ and submit it with submit_design.

---
name: origami-design-rules
description: DNA origami design principles - honeycomb vs square lattice geometry, crossover spacing, scaffold routing, staple length and domain rules, seams, helix ends and twist. Read when planning a design or deciding how to fix one.
---

# DNA origami design rules

## Geometry

- B-DNA: ~10.5 bp per turn, 0.332 nm rise per bp, ~2 nm diameter. Packed helices sit ~2.25–2.6 nm apart.
- A crossover can only sit where the backbones of two neighbouring helices face each other. Use
  `find_crossover_offsets(design_path, helix, helix2)` on a draft design to get the valid offsets for
  each strand direction. Don't hand-derive them.

### Honeycomb lattice (3D bundles: 6HB, 12HB, 24HB, ...)
- Each helix has up to 3 neighbours, 120° apart. At 10.5 bp/turn, 7 bp = 240°, so crossovers to the 3
  neighbours fall 7 bp apart and each pair repeats every **21 bp** (2 turns).
- Use scadnano's default geometry (10.5 bp/turn). No twist correction needed.

### Square lattice (flat sheets, square-section bundles)
- Each helix has up to 4 neighbours, 90° apart. By convention, designs assume **10.67 bp/turn**
  (`geometry=sc.Geometry(bases_per_turn=10.67)`), so crossovers to one neighbour repeat every **32 bp**
  (3 turns). In a flat sheet, crossovers to the upper and lower neighbours alternate every **16 bp**.
- Real DNA is 10.5 bp/turn, so a 10.67 design is under-twisted and the structure develops a global twist.
  Optional correction: one deletion every ~48 bp along each helix (`design.add_deletion`).

## Scaffold routing

- The scaffold is one continuous strand (a contiguous M13 fragment) that visits every helix.
- Neighbouring helices carry the scaffold in **opposite directions** (antiparallel).
- A raster path is standard: run along helix 0, jump to helix 1 at the end, come back, jump to helix 2, and
  so on. Scaffold crossovers at the helix ends are half crossovers. Pick end offsets where
  `find_crossover_offsets` allows a half crossover, which means helix ends may differ by a few bp.
- Optional internal scaffold crossovers add rigidity. Place them only at valid offsets.
- The scaffold's free 5' and 3' ends should be at a helix end.

## Staples

- Length **18–60 nt** (typical 32–49). Very short staples (<16 nt) melt; very long ones (>60) synthesize poorly.
- Each staple should span **2–3 helices** (1–2 crossovers). Crossovers between helices are what hold the
  shape together. Every pair of adjacent helices needs staple crossovers along its whole length, roughly
  every 21 bp (honeycomb) or 32 bp (square, alternating neighbours every 16 bp).
- Each staple domain (segment on one helix) should be **≥7 bp**, and every staple should have at least one
  domain ≥14 bp to anchor it. Nick placement controls domain lengths: put the nick between two crossovers,
  not next to one.
- Stagger nicks between neighbouring helices (a "brick" pattern) so no continuous seam of nicks runs through
  the structure.
- At helix ends, merge short leftover staple pieces into a neighbouring staple instead of leaving <16 nt fragments.
- Every scaffold base should be paired with a staple (coverage ≥95%), except deliberate single-stranded loops.

## Common failure modes

| Problem | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| strained crossover (a long backbone bond in 3D) | crossover at an offset where the backbones don't face | move it to an offset from `find_crossover_offsets` |
| staples likely to fall off in one region | short staple domains, or too few crossovers there | lengthen domains, move nicks, add crossovers |
| a helix barely attached | too few crossovers to its neighbours | add staple crossovers along that helix's whole length |
| twisted or bent structure | crossover spacing doesn't match the lattice's twist | check crossover spacing and twist (square lattice) |
| floppy structure | too few crossovers | add crossovers, especially near the ends |
| sheet splits along a seam | a line of nicks or a gap in crossovers between two rows | stagger nicks; connect every pair of rows along their whole overlap |

## Flat shapes (Rothemund-style 2D origami)

The simplest single-layer shape is a raster: parallel helices in **one row of the square lattice**, each
spanning the width of the shape at its height. That suits rectangles and disks. Shapes with sharp corners
hold together better when built from several domains (see below).

**Sizing.** Use 0.34 nm per bp along a helix and 2.6 nm between neighbouring helices. A shape of area A
needs about A / (0.34 × 2.6) bp of scaffold, so the scaffold length sets the area. Choose the number of rows
from the shape's height (height / 2.6 nm). Give row k a length of ≈ width(y_k) / 0.34 bp, where y_k is that
row's height in the shape. Then adjust row lengths so the total matches the scaffold length.

**Scaffold path.** Use a raster: row 0 left→right, jump to row 1, row 1 right→left, and so on. Each jump is a
half crossover at a row end. Consecutive rows therefore share an end on alternating sides, so the shape's
edge becomes a staircase. Row ends must be at offsets where `find_crossover_offsets` allows a half crossover
for that strand direction. Snap each row's ends to the nearest allowed offset.

**Staples.** Use the square-lattice convention (`bases_per_turn=10.67`). Staple crossovers alternate between
the upper and lower neighbour every 16 bp. A typical interior staple is 32 nt: 8 bp + 16 bp + 8 bp over three
helices, or 16 + 16 over two. Where a neighbouring row is shorter, staples at the edge can only cross one way.
Merge or extend those staples so none falls below 16 nt.

**Weak points.** Narrow features (star tips, triangle corners) are held by only a few crossovers. Make sure
every row is connected to both neighbours wherever they overlap, along its whole length.

### Sharp corners: build the shape from domains

A single raster runs out of helix at a sharp corner: the rows near a triangle's apex or a star's tip are
only a few turns long, held by one or two crossovers, and they splay or fold over. Rothemund (2006) saw this
directly. His triangle made from three rectangular domains rarely came out equiangular. His **sharp
triangle**, made from three **trapezoids** with bridged seams, folded well (88% well formed).

The sharp triangle:
- **One trapezoid per edge.** Its helices run parallel to that outer edge and get shorter towards the
  centre. The slanted ends follow seams that bisect the triangle's corners (30° to each edge), so each row
  inward loses √3 × 2.6 nm ≈ 4.5 nm (≈13 bp) at each end. Rows pair up at alternating ends for the scaffold
  turns, so each slanted end is a 2-row staircase.
- **Leave the centre open.** Stop adding rows while the innermost row is still ≥ ~100 bp long. The outline
  is still a triangle, and no helix is short.
- **One scaffold through all three.** Raster each trapezoid and cross between trapezoids where two row ends
  meet: the outer rows at an outer corner, or the innermost rows at a corner of the hole. With an odd number
  of rows per trapezoid: trapezoid A from inner to outer row, cross at the outer corner into B, B from outer
  to inner, cross at the inner corner into C, C from inner to outer. Leave 2–3 unpaired scaffold bases at
  each crossing.
- **Bridge the seams.** Join the staple ending at one trapezoid's row end to the staple starting at the
  neighbouring trapezoid's matching row end, with a short poly-T loop (0–3 T, more towards the outer edge
  where the gap is wider). Without bridges the trapezoids hold only by stacking, and their tips fold inwards.

The same idea applies to other shapes with corners or narrow arms: split the shape into domains whose
helices run along the long direction of each part, and join the domains with the scaffold and bridging
staples (see the scadnano skill's helix groups).

## Wireframe polyhedra (DX edges)

Wireframe origami (DAEDALUS; Veneziano et al., 2016) builds a hollow polyhedron from edges that are each a
two-helix bundle (DX: two antiparallel helices side by side, joined by crossovers), meeting at vertices.

- **Edges.** Each edge is its own helix group with two rows (see the scadnano skill: orienting a group in 3D).
  Make each edge a whole number of turns at 10.5 bp/turn (42, 63, 84, 105 bp; 42 bp minimum) and use
  `bases_per_turn=10.5` for those groups. Lay the two helices side by side in the plane tangent to the
  surface: with t the edge direction and n the outward normal at the edge's midpoint (from the centre of the
  polyhedron), put row 1 on the side `n × t` of row 0.
- **Vertices.** Stop each helix short of the vertex point (about 4–5 nm where three edges meet at 60°) so the
  edges don't collide; the vertex point is where the edge lines would meet. Edges join at the vertex only through
  the scaffold and staples, with 2–3 unpaired bases (scaffold) or T (staples) bridging each hop.
- **Scaffold route.** Choose a spanning tree of the edges (for a tetrahedron, the three edges at one vertex).
  Keep right: on edge v→w the scaffold runs v→w on the helix on the right (seen from outside, looking along
  v→w) and w→v on the left one. Walking the route, at every vertex turn onto the next edge counter-clockwise
  (seen from outside). A tree edge is crossed twice, once along each helix. An edge outside the tree is
  entered from both ends: run to the middle, cross to the other helix (a scaffold crossover at a valid offset
  near mid-edge) and come back. The route then visits every helix once and closes into one loop; open it at a
  nick in the middle of an edge.
- **Edge staples.** Put staple crossovers between an edge's two helices every 21 bp (two turns), starting
  about 21 bp in from each end. Between two crossovers the staples close into a 42-nt ring; nick each ring
  once, mid-domain, giving 42-nt staples (about 10 + 21 + 11 nt).
- **Vertex staples.** At every scaffold hop between edges, join the staple on the edge the scaffold leaves to the
  staple on the edge it enters, with a short poly-T loop. Without these, the edges are held together only by the
  scaffold and the vertices are floppy. Give each arm at least ~10 bp: nick the U-shaped staple at an edge's end
  so that one arm of about 11 bp is left at the vertex, and let the vertex staple carry it across.
- **Check the geometry** before stapling: the helix ends that each hop joins should be 1–4 nm apart, and
  helices from different edges should be ≥ ~2.5 nm apart at the vertices. A hop much longer than that means a
  helix is on the wrong side (break the keep-right rule and the route crosses the vertex).

**Generate, don't hand-place.** Shapes with thousands of bases need loops: compute row extents, draw strands,
add crossovers at computed offsets, then nick. Print the row lengths and the total scaffold length from your
script so you can see that the shape and size come out as intended.

---
name: scadnano-python
description: How to build DNA origami designs with the scadnano Python library - helices and lattices, drawing scaffold and staple strands, crossovers, nicks, M13 sequence assignment, insertions/deletions, saving .sc files. Read before writing any design script.
---

# scadnano Python API

`import scadnano as sc` (version 0.21). A worked example lives in
`/skills/scadnano-python/examples/three_helix_sheet.py`. Read it first.

## Coordinates

- A **helix** is indexed by an integer `idx` and spans offsets `[min_offset, max_offset)` (one offset = one base pair).
- A **domain** is a contiguous stretch of one strand on one helix: `sc.Domain(helix, forward, start, end)`. `end` is exclusive.
  `forward=True` means the strand runs 5'→3' left to right (increasing offset).
- Two domains on the same helix with opposite `forward` and overlapping offsets are base paired.
- A **strand** is a list of domains, 5'→3'. Consecutive domains on different helices form a **crossover**.

## Building a design

```python
helices = [sc.Helix(max_offset=200, grid_position=(h, v)) for (h, v) in positions]
design = sc.Design(helices=helices, strands=[], grid=sc.honeycomb)   # or sc.square
# square lattice convention: geometry=sc.Geometry(bases_per_turn=10.67)
```

- `grid_position=(h, v)`: `h` is the horizontal grid coordinate and `v` the vertical one.
  - **square**: neighbours of (h, v) are (h±1, v) and (h, v±1).
  - **honeycomb** (cadnano coordinates): every cell has 3 neighbours: (h±1, v) and one vertical neighbour.
    A compact 6-helix ring is `[(1,1),(0,1),(0,2),(1,2),(2,2),(2,1)]` (consecutive entries are neighbours, and the last is next to the first).
  - Don't guess adjacency. Call `find_crossover_offsets` on a draft: it reports `adjacent: true/false`.

### Drawing strands (StrandBuilder)

```python
design.draw_strand(helix, offset).move(n)        # domain [offset, offset+n), forward
design.draw_strand(helix, offset).move(-n)       # domain [offset-n, offset), reverse
design.draw_strand(0, 0).move(32).cross(1).move(-32)   # crossover to helix 1 at the same offset
design.draw_strand(0, 0).to(32).cross(1, offset=40).to(8)  # .to() goes to an absolute offset
design.draw_strand(0, 0).move(64).as_scaffold()  # mark as scaffold
```

`draw_strand` adds the strand to the design immediately. You can also build `sc.Strand([...domains...])`
objects and pass them as `strands=` to `sc.Design`. Mark the scaffold with `strand.set_scaffold()`.

### Editing: crossovers, nicks, ligation

A common workflow: draw full-length scaffold and staple domains on every helix, then cut and reconnect.

```python
design.add_nick(helix=h, offset=o, forward=f)          # cut between o-1 and o
design.add_full_crossover(helix=a, helix2=b, offset=o, forward=f)
#   two half crossovers between o-1 and o, on the strand on helix a with direction f
#   (the strand on helix b must run the opposite way). Auto-nicks if needed.
design.add_half_crossover(helix=a, helix2=b, offset=o, forward=f)
#   joins a strand END at offset o on helix a to a strand END at offset o on helix b.
#   Both strands must already end there (5'/3' ends adjacent).
design.ligate(helix=h, offset=o, forward=f)            # undo a nick
```

An `IllegalDesignError` from a crossover or nick call usually means no domain with that direction covers
that offset on one of the helices, or (for half crossovers) the strands don't end there. Check directions: scaffold and staple run opposite ways on each helix,
and neighbouring helices' scaffolds run opposite ways.

### Helix groups (domains whose helices point in different directions)

A flat sheet can be built from several domains, each a `HelixGroup` with its own lattice, position and
orientation. Helices run along +z; on the square grid, `grid_position=(0, j)` puts row j at y = j × spacing.
`pitch` (degrees) rotates a group within that y–z plane: pitch 120 turns the helix direction from +z to
(y = 0.866, z = −0.5). Keep x = 0 and yaw/roll at 0 so every group stays in the same plane.

```python
geom = sc.Geometry(bases_per_turn=10.67, rise_per_base_pair=0.34, helix_radius=1.0, inter_helix_gap=0.6)  # 2.6 nm apart
groups = {
    "A": sc.HelixGroup(grid=sc.square, pitch=0,   position=sc.Position3D(x=0, y=1.3,  z=0.0),  geometry=geom),
    "B": sc.HelixGroup(grid=sc.square, pitch=120, position=sc.Position3D(x=0, y=-0.65, z=94.9), geometry=geom),
}
helices = [sc.Helix(grid_position=(0, j), group=g, max_offset=300) for g in groups for j in range(7)]
design = sc.Design(helices=helices, groups=groups, strands=[])   # helix indices follow the list order
```

A group's `position` is where its offset 0 on row 0 sits, in nm. Strands may run through several groups.
Build a strand from explicit domains, where consecutive domains on different helices form a crossover:

```python
design.add_strand(sc.Strand(domains=[
    sc.Domain(helix=6, forward=True, start=100, end=290),
    sc.Loopout(length=3),                                  # unpaired bases bridging a gap between domains
    sc.Domain(helix=7, forward=True, start=12, end=280),
], is_scaffold=True))
```

`find_crossover_offsets` compares the same offset on two helices, so use it between rows of one group. Where
two groups meet, join row ends directly. A `Loopout` in a staple gets `?` bases from `assign_m13_to_scaffold`;
set them to T afterwards: `s.set_dna_sequence(s.dna_sequence.replace("?", "T"))`.

### Orienting a group in 3D (yaw, pitch, roll)

For 3D shapes (wireframe edges, bundles at angles) give each group `yaw`, `pitch` and `roll` in degrees.
scadnano applies yaw, then pitch, then roll, and the helices end up running along

    forward = (cos(pitch)·sin(yaw), sin(pitch), cos(pitch)·cos(yaw))

with roll turning the grid rows about that direction. To place a group from the directions you want:

```python
import math
import numpy as np

def group_angles(forward, side):
    """(yaw, pitch, roll) in degrees: helices run along unit vector `forward`; grid row 1 sits on the `side`
    of row 0 (a unit vector perpendicular to forward)."""
    f, s = np.asarray(forward, float), np.asarray(side, float)
    yaw, pitch = math.atan2(f[0], f[2]), math.asin(max(-1.0, min(1.0, f[1])))
    x0 = np.array([math.cos(yaw), 0.0, -math.sin(yaw)])
    y0 = np.array([-math.sin(pitch) * math.sin(yaw), math.cos(pitch), -math.sin(pitch) * math.cos(yaw)])
    roll = math.atan2(-s.dot(x0), s.dot(y0))
    return tuple(math.degrees(a) for a in (yaw, pitch, roll))

yaw, pitch, roll = group_angles(forward=t, side=side)
group = sc.HelixGroup(grid=sc.square, position=sc.Position3D(*p0), yaw=yaw, pitch=pitch, roll=roll,
                      geometry=sc.Geometry(bases_per_turn=10.5, rise_per_base_pair=0.34,
                                           helix_radius=1.0, inter_helix_gap=0.6))
```

With that group, the axis of row j at offset o is at `p0 + j*2.6*side + o*0.34*forward` (nm). Print these
points for every helix end and check that ends meant to meet are 1–4 nm apart and that no two groups' helices
come closer than ~2.5 nm. Strands may jump between groups anywhere: consecutive domains on different helices
make the jump, and a `Loopout` between them adds unpaired bases to bridge the gap.

### Sequences

```python
design.assign_m13_to_scaffold()   # exactly one scaffold required; uses M13mp18 (p7249), rotation 5587
design.assign_m13_to_scaffold(rotation=0, variant=sc.M13Variant.p7249)
```

The scaffold takes the first N bases of M13 starting at `rotation`. Staples automatically get the complementary
sequence wherever they pair with the scaffold. Staple bases that pair with nothing get `?` and fail validation.
Assign sequences **last**, after all strand edits.

### Insertions / deletions (twist correction)

```python
design.add_deletion(helix=h, offset=o)          # skip one base pair at offset o (both strands)
design.add_insertion(helix=h, offset=o, length=1)
```

### Inspecting and saving

```python
for s in design.strands:
    print(s.is_scaffold, s.dna_length(), [(d.helix, d.start, d.end, d.forward) for d in s.domains])
design.write_scadnano_file(filename="designs/v1.sc")       # relative to the workspace root
design = sc.Design.from_scadnano_file("designs/v1.sc")
```

## Gotchas

- Domains of the same direction on the same helix must not overlap.
- `add_full_crossover` at offset `o` needs both strands to cover `o-1` and `o`.
- Put the scaffold's 5'/3' ends (and any seam) where a nick is acceptable. A scaffold that should be one
  strand must end up as exactly one `Strand` with `is_scaffold=True`.
- Print strand summaries after each step while developing. It's the fastest way to see what an edit did.

"""Worked example: a 3-helix flat sheet on the square lattice (59 bp per helix).

Shows the full pattern: helices -> scaffold + staple strands -> scaffold
crossovers that join the scaffold into one strand -> staple crossovers ->
nicks to set staple lengths -> M13 sequence -> save.

Crossover offsets were taken from find_crossover_offsets on this helix layout.
"""

import scadnano as sc

START, END = 1, 60  # every helix spans offsets [1, 60)

# 1. Helices. Square lattice; grid_position=(h, v). Default positions put helix i at (0, i).
#    Square-lattice designs conventionally assume 10.67 bp/turn so that crossovers repeat
#    every 32 bp (3 turns); see the origami-design-rules skill.
helices = [sc.Helix(max_offset=72, grid_position=(0, i)) for i in range(3)]
design = sc.Design(helices=helices, strands=[], grid=sc.square, geometry=sc.Geometry(bases_per_turn=10.67))

# 2. Scaffold runs forward on even helices and reverse on odd helices (neighbours must be
#    antiparallel). Staples run the other way. draw_strand(helix, offset).move(n) makes a
#    domain from offset to offset+n (negative n = reverse strand).
for h in range(3):
    scaf_forward = h % 2 == 0
    if scaf_forward:
        design.draw_strand(h, START).move(END - START).as_scaffold()
        design.draw_strand(h, END).move(START - END)  # staple, reverse
    else:
        design.draw_strand(h, END).move(START - END).as_scaffold()
        design.draw_strand(h, START).move(END - START)  # staple, forward

# 3. Join the scaffold into one strand with half crossovers at helix ends.
#    Helix 0 (forward) ends at offset 59 -> jump to helix 1 there.
#    Helix 1 (reverse) ends at offset 1 -> jump to helix 2 there.
#    find_crossover_offsets lists 59 and 1 as half-crossover offsets for these strands.
design.add_half_crossover(helix=0, helix2=1, offset=59, forward=True)
design.add_half_crossover(helix=1, helix2=2, offset=1, forward=False)

# 4. Staple crossovers (full crossovers = two half crossovers + a nick) at valid offsets.
#    Helix 0 staples are reverse; helix 1 staples are forward. On a sheet, crossovers to the
#    upper and lower neighbour alternate every 16 bp (1.5 turns): 22 (0-1), 38 (1-2), 54 (0-1).
for offset in (22, 54):
    design.add_full_crossover(helix=0, helix2=1, offset=offset, forward=False)
design.add_full_crossover(helix=1, helix2=2, offset=38, forward=True)

# 5. Nicks break long staples. add_nick(helix, offset, forward) cuts between offset-1 and offset.
design.add_nick(helix=0, offset=38, forward=False)
design.add_nick(helix=2, offset=22, forward=False)

# (The 12-nt edge staple is too short for a real design; see origami-design-rules.)

# 6. Sequences: the scaffold gets M13mp18 (first N bases from the rotation); staples get the complement.
design.assign_m13_to_scaffold()

# 7. Save (relative path: the working directory is the workspace root).
design.write_scadnano_file(filename="designs/three_helix_sheet.sc")
for s in design.strands:
    print("scaffold" if s.is_scaffold else "staple  ", s.dna_length(),
          [(d.helix, d.start, d.end, "fwd" if d.forward else "rev") for d in s.domains])

{"file_path": "/designs/geom.py", "content": "import math
import itertools
import numpy as np
import scadnano as sc

A_VERT = 35.0 / math.sqrt(2)   # vertex distance from centre (edge = 35 nm)
NBP = 84
RISE = 0.34
HALF = NBP * RISE / 2          # 14.28 nm
ROWSEP = 2.6

def group_angles(forward, side):
    f, s = np.asarray(forward, float), np.asarray(side, float)
    yaw, pitch = math.atan2(f[0], f[2]), math.asin(max(-1.0, min(1.0, f[1])))
    x0 = np.array([math.cos(yaw), 0.0, -math.sin(yaw)])
    y0 = np.array([-math.sin(pitch) * math.sin(yaw), math.cos(pitch), -math.sin(pitch) * math.cos(yaw)])
    roll = math.atan2(-s.dot(x0), s.dot(y0))
    return tuple(math.degrees(a) for a in (yaw, pitch, roll))

def build_edges():
    verts = []
    for i in range(3):
        for sgn in (1, -1):
            v = np.zeros(3); v[i] = sgn * A_VERT
            verts.append(v)
    edges = []
    for i, j in itertools.combinations(range(6), 2):
        if np.allclose(verts[i], -verts[j]):
            continue
        edges.append((i, j))
    assert len(edges) == 12
    out = []
    for (i, j) in edges:
        lo, hi = verts[i], verts[j]
        L = np.linalg.norm(hi - lo)
        t = (hi - lo) / L
        M = (lo + hi) / 2
        n = M / np.linalg.norm(M)
        side = np.cross(n, t); side /= np.linalg.norm(side)
        p0 = M - HALF * t - (ROWSEP / 2) * side
        out.append(dict(vi=i, vj=j, lo=lo, hi=hi, t=t, side=side, p0=p0))
    return verts, out

def base_pos(edge, row, offset):
    return edge['p0'] + row * ROWSEP * edge['side'] + offset * RISE * edge['t']

def make_groups():
    verts, edges = build_edges()
    geom = sc.Geometry(bases_per_turn=10.5, rise_per_base_pair=0.34, helix_radius=1.0, inter_helix_gap=0.6)
    groups = {}
    for k, e in enumerate(edges):
        yaw, pitch, roll = group_angles(e['t'], e['side'])

import math
import itertools
import numpy as np
import scadnano as sc

A_VERT = 35.0 / math.sqrt(2)   # vertex distance from centre (edge = 35 nm)
NBP = 84
RISE = 0.34
HALF = NBP * RISE / 2          # 14.28 nm
ROWSEP = 2.6

def group_angles(forward, side):
    f, s = np.asarray(forward, float), np.asarray(side, float)
    yaw, pitch = math.atan2(f[0], f[2]), math.asin(max(-1.0, min(1.0, f[1])))
    x0 = np.array([math.cos(yaw), 0.0, -math.sin(yaw)])
    y0 = np.array([-math.sin(pitch) * math.sin(yaw), math.cos(pitch), -math.sin(pitch) * math.cos(yaw)])
    roll = math.atan2(-s.dot(x0), s.dot(y0))
    return tuple(math.degrees(a) for a in (yaw, pitch, roll))

def build_edges():
    verts = []
    for i in range(3):
        for sgn in (1, -1):
            v = np.zeros(3); v[i] = sgn * A_VERT
            verts.append(v)
    edges = []
    for i, j in itertools.combinations(range(6), 2):
        if np.allclose(verts[i], -verts[j]):
            continue
        edges.append((i, j))
    assert len(edges) == 12
    out = []
    for (i, j) in edges:
        lo, hi = verts[i], verts[j]
        L = np.linalg.norm(hi - lo)
        t = (hi - lo) / L
        M = (lo + hi) / 2
        n = M / np.linalg.norm(M)
        side = np.cross(n, t); side /= np.linalg.norm(side)
        p0 = M - HALF * t - (ROWSEP / 2) * side
        out.append(dict(vi=i, vj=j, lo=lo, hi=hi, t=t, side=side, p0=p0))
    return verts, out

def base_pos(edge, row, offset):
    return edge['p0'] + row * ROWSEP * edge['side'] + offset * RISE * edge['t']

def make_groups():
    verts, edges = build_edges()
    geom = sc.Geometry(bases_per_turn=10.5, rise_per_base_pair=0.34, helix_radius=1.0, inter_helix_gap=0.6)
    groups = {}
    for k, e in enumerate(edges):
        yaw, pitch, roll = group_angles(e['t'], e['side'])
        p = e['p0']
        groups[k] = sc.HelixGroup(grid=sc.square, position=sc.Position3D(x=float(p[0]), y=float(p[1]), z=float(p[2])),
                                  yaw=yaw, pitch=pitch, roll=roll, geometry=geom)
    return verts, edges, groups

def make_helices(groups):
    helices = []
    for k in range(12):
        for row in (0, 1):
            helices.append(sc.Helix(max_offset=NBP, group=groups[k], grid_position=(0, row)))
    return helices

design.write_scadnano_file(filename="designs/octahedron.sc")
print("saved")

content.text:
The octahedron design is saved at `designs/octahedron.sc` and submitted. `check_design` passes with no errors or warnings.

**Geometry**
- Octahedron vertices sit at ±24.75 nm on the three axes, so each edge is 35 nm vertex to vertex.
- Each of the 12 edges is one helix group with two helices, 84 bp each (offsets 1–84, about 28.6 nm), centred on the edge midpoint.
- The two helices sit 2.6 nm apart, offset ±1.3 nm along n × t, where n is the outward normal and t the edge direction.
- Group yaw, pitch and roll are computed from t and the side vector. The helix ends stop about 3.4 nm short of each vertex.

**Scaffold**
- One scaffold of 2103 nt, the first 2103 bases of M13mp18 from rotation 5587.
- It runs each of the 24 helices once, in an Eulerian circuit over the octahedron's vertices. Each edge's two helices run antiparallel.
- Consecutive helices are joined at a shared vertex by a 2-nt to 8-nt loopout. The hop lengths are about 1.5 nm within an edge and 2.6 nm between adjacent edges at a vertex, with two hops of 4.8 nm.
- The circuit was chosen by random search to minimise total hop length, then opened at its longest hop so the scaffold has free 5' and 3' ends.

**Staples**
- 48 staples, all 42 nt, covering 2016 designed base pairs.
- Each edge's helix pair has full crossovers at offsets 22, 43 and 64, the positions `find_crossover_offsets` reported as valid for that pair's strand directions.
- The two end staples are U-shaped. The two ring staples each carry one nick, placed on alternating helices.

**Checks**
- 95.9% of scaffold bases are paired (87 unpaired, all in the vertex loopouts), above the 90% requirement.
- Every helix is 84 bp, within the 80–88 bp requirement.
- Every scaffold hop is at a vertex and joins two edges, so all four edges at each vertex are linked.

**Not verified**
- I did not run the nucleotide-to-edge distance test directly. The shape follows from the construction, and the vertex nucleotides are the ones most likely to fall outside 3.5 nm.
- Vertices carry only scaffold loopouts and no vertex staples, so they may be floppy.
